questions.stem: A billing API on Java 21 receives the text "2026-10-05T23:15:00-04:00" and passes it to Instant.parse. What does the call produce?

options.text: The instant 2026-10-06T03:15:00Z, since the offset in the text is applied and the result is in UTC
options.says: Instant.parse reads a Z or a numeric offset and converts the time to UTC: 23:15 at -04:00 is 03:15 the next day in UTC

options.text: The instant 2026-10-05T23:15:00Z, since the offset in the text is read and the clock time is kept as UTC
options.says: the offset is not dropped; the page's run turns 10:30+01:00 into 09:30Z

options.text: A DateTimeParseException, since the text has to end in Z for Instant.parse to accept it
options.says: Instant.parse accepts a numeric offset as well as Z, and refuses only text with neither

options.text: A DateTimeParseException, since the text has to name a region such as America/New_York for Instant.parse to accept it
options.says: a numeric offset is enough, and a trailing region id is refused rather than required

origin.section: Instant.parse Accepts Only Text That Names Its Offset

questions.stem: A test builds Instant t = Instant.ofEpochMilli(-1_250). What do t.getEpochSecond() and t.getNano() return?

options.text: -1 and -250,000,000, since each part keeps the sign of the whole value
options.says: the nanosecond part is never negative; it is always between 0 and 999,999,999

options.text: -1 and 250,000,000, since the seconds part carries the sign and the nanoseconds the rest
options.says: -1 s plus 0.25 s is -0.75 s, not -1.25 s; the seconds must go down to -2 so that a non-negative nano part can make up the rest

options.text: -2 and 750,000,000, since the seconds round towards the past and the nanoseconds count forward from there
options.says: the nano part is always 0 to 999,999,999, so -1.25 s is second -2 plus 0.75 s, as -0.5 s is second -1 plus 0.5 s

options.text: -2 and -250,000,000, since the seconds round towards the past and the nanoseconds keep the sign of the rest
options.says: the nanosecond part is never negative, and -2 s minus 0.25 s would be -2.25 s anyway

origin.section: An Instant Is Seconds and Nanoseconds Counted From 1970-01-01T00:00Z

questions.stem: An audit store keeps each record until created.plus(1, ChronoUnit.YEARS), where created is an Instant. The code is deployed and the purge job runs for the first time. What happens?

options.text: Each record is kept 365 days, since a year added to an instant counts as 365 times 86,400 seconds
options.says: only units up to DAYS have a fixed length for Instant; YEARS is unsupported and throws

options.text: Each record is kept 365 or 366 days, since the instant's UTC date tells whether a leap day lies in between
options.says: an Instant has no calendar fields to consult; YEARS throws UnsupportedTemporalTypeException

options.text: The code never deploys, since the compiler accepts only a Duration as the amount added to an instant
options.says: plus(long, TemporalUnit) compiles for any unit; the refusal comes when it runs

options.text: The job fails on its first record, since an instant has no calendar from which to take the length of a year
options.says: plus with MONTHS or YEARS throws UnsupportedTemporalTypeException at run time; the length of a year needs a calendar and a zone

origin.section: An Instant Has No Calendar, So Months Need a Zone

questions.stem: An order service on Java 21 on Linux sets placedAt = Instant.now(), caches the order under a key that includes placedAt, and publishes placedAt.toEpochMilli() in an event. A consumer in the same JVM rebuilds Instant.ofEpochMilli(...) from the event and looks the order up in the cache. What does the lookup do?

options.text: It misses the order nearly every time, since placedAt has digits below the millisecond that the event drops
options.says: toEpochMilli drops the sub-millisecond digits, so the rebuilt instant differs from the one in the key unless placedAt was truncated when it was stamped

options.text: It misses the order only now and then, since two readings of the clock can differ by a few nanoseconds
options.says: the clock is read once, when placedAt is stamped; the difference comes from the truncation in toEpochMilli, which affects nearly every stamp

options.text: It finds the order, since Instant.now() returns whole milliseconds just as System.currentTimeMillis() does
options.says: on Java 21 on Linux, Instant.now() fills digits below the millisecond in nearly every call

options.text: It finds the order, since equals on two instants compares them to the millisecond
options.says: equals compares seconds and nanoseconds; the page's round trip is unequal by 456789 ns

origin.section: A Timestamp Survives a Store Only at the Store's Precision
